title: Last words
hookLine: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah enters the garden (Abu Dawud)
carry: let these be my last words
last: THE CALL, AS EACH HEARS IT.

lines: A FEW WORDS, NEAR HER EAR.
A LIGHT LEFT ON IN THE HALLWAY.
cards: A room late at night, the lamp turned low. An old woman in the bed, her breathing slow and uneven.
Her son sits close and, every so often, without any pressure in his voice, says a few words near her ear: la ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. He isn't quizzing her.
He's leaving the words in the air, the way you'd leave a light on in the hallway, in case she wants to reach for them. Then he goes quiet again, and the room holds the words with him.

teach.b: The son is following two sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The first is in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 3116: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter the garden.
The second is in Sahih Muslim, number 916: prompt your dying with la ilaha illallah. The word for that gentle prompting is talqin.
Scholars who explain it advise doing it softly, saying the words rather than ordering the dying person to repeat them, and not pressing if they've already said them.

teach.h: AN OPEN DOOR, NOT A TEST.
teach.b: An open door, not a test. Now turn it around.
Nobody chooses the hour. So how does anyone make sure of their last words? Sahih al-Bukhari, number 247, gives one answer.
The Prophet ﷺ told a companion: when you go to bed, make wudu as for prayer, lie on your right side, and say a short supplication handing yourself over to God.
If you die that night, he said, you die on the natural way, and he told him to make those words the last thing he said.
Sleep, in this teaching, is a small cousin of death; the Qur'an, at 39:42, speaks of God taking souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died, in their sleep.
Some Muslims join these teachings and say the shahada as the very last thing before sleep, night after night, so the words are well worn by the time they're needed.

how: Muslims at a deathbed often say la ilaha illallah softly near the dying person, a practice called talqin, and some say the shahada or the bedtime supplication taught in the hadith as the last words before sleep.

o: a will read aloud to the family after the funeral
a prayer the family says for someone after death
the shahada at life's end, gently prompted by loved ones

p: souls taken at death and in sleep

s: talqin means pressing the dying person to repeat the words
scholars who explain it say to say the words softly, not to order or keep pressing.
a hadith ties bedtime words to dying on the natural way
Bukhari 247: if you die that night after saying them, you die on the natural way.
the Qur'an links sleep and death in one verse
39:42 speaks of souls taken at death, and of those not yet dead, in their sleep.

games.q: you're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and you want to help them with the words la ilaha illallah. what does the teaching on talqin suggest?
o: ask them again and again to repeat it.
say it softly near them, and don't keep pressing.
stay silent, since it's not your place.
games.why: talqin is a gentle prompt: say the words softly, leave them in the air, and stop pressing once they've said them.

practice: Sit or lie as you might at bedtime, and let the day go out of your shoulders.
If you're Muslim and you pray, say la ilaha illallah slowly, once, and let the quiet hold it; if not, sit with the question the son was answering: what words do I want close by at the end?
If this brings up grief or a heaviness that won't lift, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Last words. In this teaching, the shahada said at the end, prompted gently by those who love you, and rehearsed every night before sleep. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: there is no god but Allah, the first half of the shahada.

carryVoice: Your line: let these be my last words. Night after night, the words grow familiar. Tomorrow, the prayer begins.
